title: Sort Three Kinds in One Pass
statement:
An array nums holds only the values 0, 1 and 2. Rearrange it in place so all the 0s come first, then all the 1s, then all the 2s.

Do not use the built-in sort. Return nothing; the checker reads nums after your function runs. Aim for a single pass with O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: Two of each kind, grouped in order.
Swapping the first 2 to the back brings in another 2. That slot must be checked again before moving on.
Already grouped; nothing should move out of place.

hints: Counting how many of each value there are and rewriting the array works in two passes. Can you place values as you meet them instead?
Keep three regions: a block of 0s at the front, a block of 2s at the back, and an unknown middle you are still scanning.
Use pointers lo, mid, hi. A 0 at mid swaps to lo (both advance). A 2 at mid swaps to hi (only hi moves back, because the value that came in is unseen). A 1 just advances mid.

explain.intuition:
Picture the array as four zones: confirmed 0s at the front [0, lo), confirmed 1s [lo, mid), an unknown zone [mid, hi], and confirmed 2s at the back (hi, n). Each step looks at nums[mid] and shrinks the unknown zone by one.

A 0 belongs at the boundary lo; swap it there. What comes back from lo is a 1 (or the same slot), which is already checked, so mid can move too. A 2 belongs at hi; swap it there and shrink hi. But the value swapped in from hi has never been looked at, so mid stays put. That asymmetry is the whole puzzle.
pitfalls: Advancing mid after swapping with hi. In [2, 2, 0] the incoming value can be another 2 or a 0 that still needs to move.
Looping while mid < hi instead of mid ≤ hi, which leaves the last unknown slot unchecked.
Returning a new sorted array instead of changing nums.

solutions.title: Count, then rewrite
solutions.idea: Count the 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass, then overwrite the array in a second pass.

solutions.title: Three pointers, one pass
solutions.idea: Grow a block of 0s from the left and a block of 2s from the right, scanning the unknown middle once.

followups: There are k kinds instead of three. Which approach still works, and what does it cost?
How does this partition step relate to quicksort on arrays with many equal keys?
